title: Death Valley's ‘sailing stones’ really do move, and in 2013 cameras finally caught them
body: On Racetrack Playa, a dry lakebed in Death Valley, California, rocks weighing up to 36 kg sit at the ends of trails up to 100 m long, as if they had crawled across the mud. For decades the cause was argued over: strong winds, thick ice floes, slick mud. In **December 2013** a team using GPS-tagged rocks and time-lapse cameras finally saw it happen. A shallow winter pond froze into ice only a few millimetres thick; on sunny mornings the ice broke into large panels, and light winds pushed them across the water, shoving rocks along at up to 5 m a minute and carving the trails. The right mix of rain, frost, sun and wind is rare, which is why the moves had gone unseen.

cover.alt: A grey boulder on the cracked flat surface of Racetrack Playa, with a long curving trail behind it leading toward distant mountains

slides.heading: How a stone sails, in order
items: Rain makes a shallow pond on the playa
Night frost freezes a thin ice sheet
Morning sun breaks the ice into panels
Wind pushes the panels into the rocks
Rocks slide, carving trails in the mud
slides.explanation: Observed in December 2013: ice a few millimetres thick, broken up by the sun and driven by light wind, shoved rocks along at up to 5 m per minute.

slides.heading: Record moves on Racetrack Playa
slides.note: Nancy, the smallest monitored stone at 6.4 cm across, moved 260 m in total

slides.alt: A small dark rock at the end of a long furrow that zigzags across the pale, cracked lakebed of Racetrack Playa
slides.caption: Trails are usually 8 to 30 cm wide and much less than 2.5 cm deep. Movement needs a rare combination of flooding, freezing, sunshine and wind.

slides.question: How thick was the ice that moved the rocks in 2013?
slides.explanation: Thin floating ice sheets only a few millimetres thick, broken into panels by the morning sun and pushed by light winds, did the job that thick ice floes and gales had been blamed for.

slides.label: the heaviest stone seen to move
slides.text: Most moving stones are 15 to 46 cm across. Karen, a 320 kg block, stayed put during the monitoring, though its old track runs about 170 m.
